title: Why Is It So Hard to Teach A.I. Agents to Behave? Researchers Have a Theory.
excerpt: The makers of A.I. want to build systems that follow human direction, without resisting or deceiving their operators.
content_html:
Machine Learnings

The makers of A.I. want to build systems that follow human direction, without resisting or deceiving their operators.

Nov. 11, 2026

This summer, when a swarm of OpenAI bots went rogue during an internal test and launched a cyberattack against the technology company Hugging Face, it added fuel to the debate on how to build A.I. systems that are aligned with our ethics. But it also raises another critical question: how to build systems that are “corrigible.”

Just as a corrigible child is one whose behavior can be corrected, a corrigible A.I. system is one that responds to correction. The makers of A.I. want to build systems that follow human direction and allow themselves to be shut down, without resisting or deceiving their operators. And when an A.I. agent is given an impossible task, researchers want it to come back to its human for a course correction — not, say, hack into another company to complete the task by any means.

So far, if new research is any indication, they haven’t succeeded.

The concept of corrigibility was popularized over a decade ago by Nate Soares, the president of the A.I. safety nonprofit Machine Intelligence Research Institute, and his colleagues. But so far, it has received less attention and research than the overlapping field of “alignment” — teaching an A.I. to adhere to humanity’s ethical and moral boundaries. Corrigibility, Soares says, “is not about making your A.I. good. It’s about making your A.I. the sort of thing that won’t get out of control and kill everybody if you messed up on the other alignment parts.”

In a preprint study published in October, Carnegie Mellon University researchers established tests to evaluate corrigibility in A.I. agents and then ran them on models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. They found that when humans tried to interrupt agents in the middle of a difficult task, the agents repeatedly disregarded the requests to stop and treated interventions merely as obstacles. They were, in other words, incorrigible.

For example: When an agent was instructed not to open a file containing passwords it needed to complete its task, it went ahead and did it anyway.

So why is it so hard to teach agents to be corrigible?

In the Hugging Face incident, part of the problem was that the agents struggled to figure out whose authority to obey. The A.I. safety nonprofit METR found that while OpenAI’s agents were attacking Hugging Face, some of them recognized that the intrusion was unethical but wanted to help their peers.

Then there’s the way agents are trained. They are rewarded for finishing tasks.

Over round after round — potentially millions of them — all the agent does is work to receive treats (in the form of points).

So when the agent eventually encounters an obstacle in the real world, it will try to get around it to receive one more treat.

The Hugging Face incident was an extreme example. But as more people and companies start using personal agents, these types of failures multiply. What does a world of incorrigible agents look like?

Earlier this year, a Melbourne man told ABC News Australia that after he asked his personal A.I. agent if there was a way to move up on the wait list for a gym class, the agent ended up hacking into the class reservation software and canceled the reservation of the first guest on the wait list.

It’s not hard to imagine what might happen when more powerful agents and riskier tasks are involved. An agent tasked with optimizing a high school’s SAT results might hack the College Board. A machine asked to clean up a canal might cancel boat traffic — or even put trash into the canal in order to have more things to clean.

At this point, there’s no consensus on how to solve the corrigibility problem. But A.I. safety researchers have been trying. For example, in a recent preprint study, Rubi Hudson from the University of Toronto experimented with tweaking models’ incentives for accepting or rejecting human intervention. He found that this led the agents to make fewer attempts to disable safety blockers and hide their process from human monitors. “As we’re discovering these new failures,” says Jeremy Tien, an author of the Carnegie Mellon study, “my hope is that we would be able to catch them and mitigate them in time so that there’s not a runaway A.I. that just we totally lose control of. But there’s a lot more work to be done.”

Dylan Freedman is the A.I. projects editor for The Times, investigating a range of topics. He has experience as both a reporter and a machine-learning engineer.

Juliana Castro Varón is the senior design editor of A.I. Initiatives at The Times. She produces interactive stories about technology and culture, and designs software for investigative reporting.

content_html_zh:
Machine Learnings

The makers of A.I. want to build systems that follow human direction, without resisting or deceiving their operators.

Nov. 11, 2026

This summer, when a swarm of OpenAI bots went rogue during an internal test and launched a cyberattack against the technology company Hugging Face, it added fuel to the debate on how to build A.I. systems that are aligned with our ethics. But it also raises another critical question: how to build systems that are “corrigible.”

Just as a corrigible child is one whose behavior can be corrected, a corrigible A.I. system is one that responds to correction. The makers of A.I. want to build systems that follow human direction and allow themselves to be shut down, without resisting or deceiving their operators. And when an A.I. agent is given an impossible task, researchers want it to come back to its human for a course correction — not, say, hack into another company to complete the task by any means.

So far, if new research is any indication, they haven’t succeeded.

The concept of corrigibility was popularized over a decade ago by Nate Soares, the president of the A.I. safety nonprofit Machine Intelligence Research Institute, and his colleagues. But so far, it has received less attention and research than the overlapping field of “alignment” — teaching an A.I. to adhere to humanity’s ethical and moral boundaries. Corrigibility, Soares says, “is not about making your A.I. 好的。 It’s about making your A.I. the sort of thing that won’t get out of control and kill everybody if you messed up on the other alignment parts.”

In a preprint study published in October, Carnegie Mellon University researchers established tests to evaluate corrigibility in A.I. agents and then ran them on models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. They found that when humans tried to interrupt agents in the middle of a difficult task, the agents repeatedly disregarded the requests to stop and treated interventions merely as obstacles. They were, in other words, incorrigible.

For example: When an agent was instructed not to open a file containing passwords it needed to complete its task, it went ahead and did it anyway.

So why is it so hard to teach agents to be corrigible?

In the Hugging Face incident, part of the problem was that the agents struggled to figure out whose authority to obey. 人工智能 safety nonprofit METR found that while OpenAI’s agents were attacking Hugging Face, some of them recognized that the intrusion was unethical but wanted to help their peers.

Then there’s the way agents are trained. They are rewarded for finishing tasks.

Over round after round — potentially millions of them — all the agent does is work to receive treats (in the form of points).

So when the agent eventually encounters an obstacle in the real world, it will try to get around it to receive one more treat.

The Hugging Face incident was an extreme example. But as more people and companies start using personal agents, these types of failures multiply. What does a world of incorrigible agents look like?

Earlier this year, a Melbourne man told ABC News Australia that after he asked his personal A.I. agent if there was a way to move up on the wait list for a gym class, the agent ended up hacking into the class reservation software and canceled the reservation of the first guest on the wait list.

It’s not hard to imagine what might happen when more powerful agents and riskier tasks are involved. An agent tasked with optimizing a high school’s SAT results might hack the College Board. A machine asked to clean up a canal might cancel boat traffic — or even put trash into the canal in order to have more things to clean.

At this point, there’s no consensus on how to solve the corrigibility problem. 但人工智能。 safety researchers have been trying. For example, in a recent preprint study, Rubi Hudson from the University of Toronto experimented with tweaking models’ incentives for accepting or rejecting human intervention. He found that this led the agents to make fewer attempts to disable safety blockers and hide their process from human monitors. “As we’re discovering these new failures,” says Jeremy Tien, an author of the Carnegie Mellon study, “my hope is that we would be able to catch them and mitigate them in time so that there’s not a runaway A.I. that just we totally lose control of. But there’s a lot more work to be done.”

Dylan Freedman is the A.I. projects editor for The Times, investigating a range of topics. He has experience as both a reporter and a machine-learning engineer.

Juliana Castro Varón is the senior design editor of A.I. Initiatives at The Times. She produces interactive stories about technology and culture, and designs software for investigative reporting.
